item.title: I'm making LLMs work on small and old devices
item.description:
Source: github.com

Top Comment:

For the last five months or so, opus and fable have both been able to do this task as a soneshot prompt. An inference engine is almost pure compute and to a first approximation the only operation your hardware needs to support to do llm inference is multiplication [the rest of an inference engine is "some trig"].

So to get any model working on $OLD_HARDWARE, the hardest part of the task is now sourcing the hardware itself and giving the agent ssh access -- a modern agent will be able to source a compiler, write the implementation, optimize it, test in qemu (or any other simulator) and push it onto the device.

Example prompt: "write an inference engine for qwen3 0.6b in pure assembly that runs on this device. Write a script to attach the weights to the resulting binary. Prefix is supplied as a stream of u32 token IDs on stdin. The engine streams u32 token IDs on stdout."

item.title: Data centers need power – lower income, rural residents pay the price
item.description:
Source: news.cornell.edu

Top Comment:

Increased demand drives up prices under a fixed supply regime. Power is, in many places of the US, something approaching a fixed supply regime. This is not a physical requirement of the universe. It is a policy choice that we have made. I would argue that it is not the data centers driving up power prices, it is our policies around how difficult it is to provision new power (or build almost anything at all) in the US.

Congress could fix this problem tomorrow. And in fact there is a bipartisan bill (BAAJA) that would go a long ways (although not all the way) towards fixing it. Now yes even if we fix these policies there would be a time lag on new generation being connected, but there is no reason to leave this problem in place.

item.title: Our software engineering interviews are changing a little
item.description:
Source: blog.janestreet.com

Top Comment:

Leetcode was stupid before LLMs and now it’s even less useful as a signal.

What I want to know is whether someone has basic DSA understanding. Is the person familiar with any programming language. Can they translate business requirements into code? Can they disambiguate weird things PMs say into a viable plan?

You do not get a better signal about that from asking harder leetcode problems.

Never once in my career has writing a tricky algorithm under time pressure been relevant. The closest thing I can think of is debugging complex systems in an outage, but then it’s more like familiarity with bash commands and general debug skills.

As for LLMs and coding, companies need to figure out how to differentiate good and bad outputs here and what lasting engineer inputs to select for. And I don’t have any idea about this.
